title: Does Starbucks Have a Secret Cheaper Size?
description:
Starbucks still makes an 8-ounce Short with the same espresso shot as a Tall, and keeping it off the menu is a classic pricing trick.
#starbucks #coffee #money #shorts

Sources: Tim Harford, Slate (Jan 6, 2006); Better Homes & Gardens via Yahoo (Apr 2019); Food Republic (Dec 2023); GOBankingRates (Jul 2025); Caffeine Informer; Starbucks fiscal 2026 results, Form 8-K (Oct 29, 2026); Finsee Q4 FY2026 review
Photos: Charles Williams, Sam Howzit, Cherrysweetdeal, cahadikin, Esparta (CC BY 2.0, Flickr)
first_comment: Be honest: did you know Starbucks had a Short size? Yes or no? ☕

scenes.say: Starbucks has a fourth, cheaper size it keeps off the menu.
scenes.source: BHG via Yahoo Apr 2019 ('Every Starbucks also has a fourth option: short'; 'isn't usually found on the menu; you have to know to ask for it'); Slate/Harford Jan 2006 (not on the menu board or website); Food Republic Dec 2023 ('may not be displayed on the Starbucks menu'); GOBankingRates Jul 2025 ('the short costs less than the tall')

scenes.say: It's called a Short: eight ounces.
scenes.source: Food Republic Dec 2023 ('smallest size you can order at 8 ounces (as opposed to a 12-ounce tall)'); Slate/Harford 2006 ('at 8 ounces, a third smaller than the smallest size on the official menu'); BHG 2019 (8 ounces)

scenes.say: Same single shot of espresso as a Tall.
scenes.source: Food Republic Dec 2023 ('All short and most tall espresso drinks made with milk will contain one shot of espresso'); Caffeine Informer (Caffe Latte: Short 75 mg, Tall 75 mg); Slate/Harford 2006 (same espresso as the tall)

scenes.say: In {2006|two thousand six}, an economist paid {$2.35|two thirty five} for one, instead of {$2.65|two sixty five}.
scenes.source: Tim Harford, 'The mystery of the short cappuccino', Slate, Jan 6 2006 ('This secret cappuccino is cheaper, too: at my local Starbucks, $2.35 instead of $2.65'). Second source for 'cheaper': GOBankingRates Jul 2025 ('the short costs less than the tall'); BHG 2019 ('often around 10 cents')

scenes.say: So why hide it? It's called price discrimination.
scenes.source: Slate/Harford 2006 (hiding the cheap option lets Starbucks charge price-sensitive customers less without losing the higher price from everyone else: 'making the cheap product invisible'); BHG 2019 (keeping the smallest size off the menu nudges customers to bigger drinks)

scenes.say: Only people who know to ask pay less. Everyone else trades up.
scenes.source: Slate/Harford 2006 ('They will serve you a better, stronger cappuccino if you want one, and they will charge you less for it'); BHG 2019 ('you have to know to ask for it')

scenes.say: Product costs are just {32¢|thirty two cents} of each Starbucks dollar, running the stores {45¢|forty five}. So bigger cups are where the profit is.
scenes.source: Starbucks FY2026 results 8-K Oct 29 2026: product and distribution costs $12,235.2M = 32.3% of $37,910.6M revenue; coffeehouse operating expenses $17,189.8M = 45.3%. Finsee Q4 FY2026 review (product and distribution costs 32.0% of revenue in Q4). Harford/Slate 2006: staff time, queue space and packaging cost about the same across sizes, so bigger drinks carry bigger markups

scenes.say: So next time, just ask for a Short. Because
